evidence.temozolomide: Stupp et al., NEJM 2005 (EORTC 26981/NCIC CE.3): RT+TMZ vs RT alone; median PFS 6.9 vs 5.0 months (overall survival HR 0.63 confirmed)
evidence.ttfields: Stupp et al., JAMA 2017 (EF-14): TTFields + TMZ vs TMZ; median PFS 6.7 vs 4.0 months (HR 0.63)
evidence.bevacizumab: Chinot et al., NEJM 2014 (AVAglio): median PFS 10.6 vs 6.2 months (HR 0.64); no overall-survival benefit (16.8 vs 16.7 months). Part of the PFS gain is imaging pseudo-response.

evidence.immunotherapy: no benefit shown in randomised glioblastoma trials; not modelled

explainer.text: The simulation was run on 150 patients, each seeded from their own tumour segmentation. For 71 of them the tumour was smaller on the second scan, so a loss rate was fitted instead of a growth rate. In 333 scan intervals from 144 patients, drug effects fitted from the records could not be separated from zero, because treatment is usually started when a tumour is already growing. For that reason the scenarios use growth-suppression effect sizes from published trials. Temozolomide is modelled as suppressing growth by 28% while the drug is active, an effect size taken from a published trial. Tumour treating fields is modelled as suppressing growth by 40% while the drug is active, an effect size taken from a published trial. Bevacizumab is modelled as suppressing growth by 42% while the drug is active, an effect size taken from a published trial. A patient's growth rate in one interval was nearly unrelated to the next (correlation -0.02 over 221 pairs), which may reflect measurement variation between scans; the scenarios are therefore what-if comparisons, not forecasts of one patient's course. A mortality risk model trained on 676 patients from three public datasets reached an AUC of 0.74 in cross-validation (0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect). All of this is a research demonstration, not a clinical tool.
